How would she have felt if she had known that her sister wanted to take away all these hopes and pleasures? Only her mother could have understood, for she would have felt almost the same. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was her mother’s one comfort after the unhappy realization that her husband never meant to go there himself.

But neither of them knew what had happened. Their delight continued almost without a pause until the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now about to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since returning, she had often been in his company, and almost all her uneasiness had passed. The feelings caused by her earlier liking for him had disappeared completely. She had even learned to see something false and tiresomely repetitive in the gentle manner that had first charmed her. His present behavior gave her a new reason to dislike him. He soon showed a wish to resume the attentions he had paid her when they first met, but after everything that had happened, these could only irritate her. Finding herself chosen for such empty, thoughtless flirting ended any concern she still felt for him. She firmly discouraged him, yet could not escape the shame of what his confidence suggested about her. He clearly believed that, however long he had ignored her and whatever his reason, he could flatter her vanity and regain her affection simply by noticing her again.

On the regiment’s final day in Meryton, he dined at Longbourn with several other officers. Elizabeth felt so little desire to part on friendly terms that, when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings. She asked whether he knew the colonel.

He looked surprised, annoyed, and alarmed. Then, recovering himself and his smile, he said that he used to see him often. He called the colonel a very gentlemanly man and asked how she had liked him. Her reply was warmly approving. Soon afterward, trying to sound unconcerned, he added, “How long did you say he stayed at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are quite different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different. But I think Mr. Darcy becomes more agreeable as you get to know him.”

“Really!” Wickham exclaimed, with a look she noticed. “And may I ask—” He stopped himself, then continued more cheerfully, “Is it his manner that improves?”

The place seemed to consist of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, giving the impression of a rather dull retreat. Wemmick’s house was a little wooden cottage among garden plots, its roofline cut and painted to resemble a battery equipped with cannons.

“My own work,” Wemmick said. “Looks pretty, doesn’t it?”

I praised it enthusiastically. I think it was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the oddest Gothic windows—most of them false—and a Gothic doorway almost too small to enter.

“That’s a proper flagpole, you see,” said Wemmick, “and on Sundays I fly a proper flag. Now look here. Once I’ve crossed this bridge, I pull it up—like this—and cut off access.”

The bridge was a plank spanning a gap about four feet wide and two feet deep. Still, it was delightful to see his pride as he raised and secured it, smiling with real pleasure instead of merely out of habit.

“At nine every night, Greenwich time,” Wemmick said, “the cannon fires. There he is, you see! And when you hear him go off, I think you’ll agree he’s a Stinger.”

The cannon in question stood in its own separate fortress, built of latticework. A clever little arrangement of tarpaulin, something like an umbrella, sheltered it from the weather.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of view, so it doesn’t spoil the effect of the fortifications—because my principle is that once you have an idea, you should carry it through and keep it going; I don’t know whether you agree—”

I said I certainly did.

“—At the back there’s a pig, along with chickens and rabbits. Then I put together my own little growing frame, you see, for cucumbers, and at supper you’ll be able to judge the sort of salad I can produce. So, sir,” Wemmick said, smiling again, though seriously too, as he shook his head, “if you imagine this little place under siege, its food supplies would let it hold out a devil of a long time.”

He then led me to an arbor about twelve yards away, reached by such cleverly winding paths that the walk took quite a while. Our glasses were already laid out in this retreat. The punch was cooling in an ornamental lake beside which the arbor stood. This circular stretch of water contained an island that might have been the salad for supper. He had installed a fountain in it that, once you started a little mill and removed a cork from a pipe, played with such force that it left the back of your hand quite wet.

“It is a curious thing, but whoever disappears is reported to have been sighted in San Francisco. It must be a charming city, endowed with all the allurements of the next world.”

“What do you suppose has become of Basil?” Dorian asked, raising his Burgundy to the light and marvelling that he could speak of the subject with such composure.

“I haven’t the faintest notion. If Basil elects to conceal himself, it is no concern of mine. If he is dead, I would rather not think of him. Death alone ever frightens me. I detest it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked wearily.

“Because,” Lord Henry replied, drawing the gilded lattice of an open vinaigrette box beneath his nose, “nowadays one can survive anything but that. Death and vulgarity are the two realities of the nineteenth century which cannot be explained away. We shall take our coffee in the music-room, Dorian. You must play me some Chopin. The man my wife eloped with played Chopin to perfection. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. Without her the house is rather solitary. Married life is, of course, only a habit—a bad habit. Yet one mourns the loss of even one’s worst habits. Perhaps those are the ones one mourns most. They form such an indispensable part of one’s character.”

Without replying, Dorian left the table and went into the adjoining room. He seated himself at the piano and allowed his fingers to wander over the white and black ivory keys. When the coffee had arrived, he paused, glanced toward Lord Henry, and said, “Harry, has it ever struck you that Basil might have been murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was immensely popular and invariably wore a Waterbury watch. Why would he be murdered? He lacked the cleverness to acquire enemies. Naturally, he possessed a remarkable genius for painting. But one may paint like Velasquez and still be altogether dull. Basil was, in fact, rather dull. Only once did he interest me: years ago, when he confessed his extravagant adoration of you and said that you were the ruling inspiration of his art.”

“I cared very much for Basil,” Dorian said, a touch of sadness in his voice. “But isn’t it said that he was murdered?”

“Oh, a few of the newspapers say so. I find it exceedingly unlikely. Paris certainly has terrible places, but Basil was hardly a man to frequent them. Curiosity was entirely lacking in him. It was his principal failing.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you I had murdered Basil?” asked the younger man.
